content.text:
Based on `BenchMutex.acquire` in `src/agentic_hil/bench.py` (lines ~366-395):

When `acquire` is called with a list of device resource keys, it processes them **in sorted order** (via `physical_resources(resources)`), calling an internal `_take(resource, deadline, stop_requested)` for each one and appending each successfully-taken resource to a local `taken` list.

If one of the requested devices is already held by another owner, `_take` raises `DeviceBusyError` (naming the current holder). At that point the method's `except BaseException` clause runs: it walks back over everything it *had* already taken in this call (`for resource in reversed(taken): self._drop(resource)`), releasing all of them, and then re-raises the exception.

So the behavior is **all-or-nothing**: if any device in the requested set is busy, `acquire` gives up every device it managed to grab earlier in that same call and raises `DeviceBusyError` — it never leaves the caller holding a partial set. This is explicitly called out in the class docstring: "`acquire` is all-or-nothing over sorted resource names, so two owners reaching for an overlapping set cannot each keep half of it."

This guarantee is also why `DeviceSet.acquire` (in `src/agentic_hil/devices.py`) deliberately passes the whole set of lock keys into a single `BenchMutex.acquire` call rather than acquiring devices one at a time — the docstring there notes: "a partially acquired set is exactly what must never escape."
